sections.content:
You know *la subida de los precios* from B2 Unit 21: a verb clause (*Los precios subieron*) can become a noun phrase. At C1 you use this to build the whole sentence around the noun phrase. It becomes the subject, and a general verb carries it: *La reducción de los desplazamientos incide en el rendimiento*. The sentence is shorter, it names the idea instead of the event, and it leaves out the doer. That is why abstracts, reports and definitions are full of it.

But there is a limit. Two phrases with *de* in a row read well; three or four make the reader go back. When that happens, return to a verb.

items.spanish: La reducción de los desplazamientos incide en el rendimiento.
items.english: The reduction in travel affects performance.

items.spanish: La validez de los resultados depende de la muestra.
items.english: The validity of the results depends on the sample.

items.spanish: La fiabilidad del método limita el alcance de la conclusión.
items.english: The reliability of the method limits the scope of the conclusion.

items.spanish: La valoración de la propuesta exige datos fiables.
items.english: The assessment of the proposal requires reliable data.

sections.content: English likes stacks of nouns: "the home working performance question". Spanish cannot stack nouns this way. Each one needs its link, usually *de*: *la cuestión del rendimiento del trabajo en casa*. A noun phrase also hides the doer. That is fine in *la validez de los resultados*, but if the reader will ask "who assessed it?", say so: *la valoración de la propuesta por el comité*, or go back to the verb.
